stage.name: How to read CORE-V core names
stage.description: A technical microcourse on CORE-V family labels, part numbers, configurations, and machine-readable identities.

scenes.title: How to read CORE-V core names

content.sceneTitle: How to read CORE-V core names
content.title: CORE-V names are a compact architecture index
content.subtitle: Decode CVE2, CV32E20, CV32E40P/X/S and CVA6 without confusing a family, repository, core, or configuration.
content.thesis: A CORE-V name narrows the search space. The specification, configuration table, release tag, and identity CSRs establish the implementation.
content.narration: CORE-V uses short labels for several different technical objects. CVE2 and CVA6 can name a family or code base. CV32E20, CV32E40X, and CV32A60AX identify more specific cores or configurations. This lesson builds a practical decoder across the embedded two-stage, embedded four-stage, and application-class six-stage lines. We will also connect the human-readable name to the repository, verified configuration, release, and the machine-readable identity CSRs.

scenes.title: First identify what kind of name you are reading

content.sceneTitle: First identify what kind of name you are reading
content.title: Family labels and part numbers answer different questions
content.subtitle: Do not compare CVE4 and CV32E40X as though they were objects at the same level.

columns.label: FAMILY / CODE-BASE LAYER
columns.title: Compact labels group an implementation line
bullets: CVE2: low-complexity two-stage embedded line and repository
CVE4: four-stage embedded family split across sibling repositories
CVA5 and CVA6: five- and six-stage application-oriented code bases
CVW: Wally-derived five-stage family with broad configuration options

columns.label: CORE / CONFIGURATION LAYER
columns.title: Longer names narrow width, class and identity
bullets: CV32E20: named two-stage MCU core produced from CVE2
CV32E40P, X and S: sibling four-stage embedded cores
CV32A60AX, CV32A60X and CV32A65X: names in the evolving CVA6 documentation set
CV64A60: the current CVA6 nomenclature example

content.takeaway: Before decoding characters, classify the object: family, repository, named core, configuration, or release.
content.narration: Start by identifying the object level. CVE2 is both a compact family label and the repository that hosts the RTL. Its current named processor is CV32E20. CVE4 is a family grouping for several four-stage cores, but CV32E40P, CV32E40X, and CV32E40S live in separate repositories. CVA6 is a heavily parameterized repository for several 32- and 64-bit cores. The longer part number narrows the implementation, but a release tag and configuration table narrow it further.

scenes.title: The grammar changed as the portfolio evolved

content.sceneTitle: The grammar changed as the portfolio evolved
content.title: Use the grammar attached to the project and date
content.subtitle: The shared fields are useful; the two historical contexts are not one universal standard.

rows.pattern: family | word length | class | identity | modifier
rows.engineeringUse: Explains the origin of CV32E40P-style names.

rows.pattern: CV | ILEN | class | pipeline stages | product ID
rows.engineeringUse: Authority for names derived from the CVA6 repository.

rows.pattern: family labels plus repository-specific core names
rows.engineeringUse: Maps the part number to the code and manual that define it.

content.note: Digits such as 2, 4, 5 and 6 often expose pipeline depth, but suffix semantics remain project-specific.
content.narration: The original OpenHW naming deck used five fields: family, word length, class, identity, and an optional modifier. There the identity combined pipeline length with a product feature number. Current CVA6 documentation publishes a related but clearer pattern: C V, instruction length, class, pipeline stages, and product identifier. Both help parse names, but neither applies blindly to every current repository. The current manual remains authoritative.

scenes.title: CVE2 and CV32E20 show the two layers cleanly

content.sceneTitle: CVE2 and CV32E20 show the two layers cleanly
content.title: CVE2 is the code base; CV32E20 is the named core
content.subtitle: The current specification turns a compact name into an implementable set of processor configurations.

columns.label: MICROARCHITECTURE
columns.title: CV32E20
bullets: 32-bit, low-complexity MCU core derived from Ibex/Zero-riscy
Two stages: instruction fetch, then combined decode/execute
Maximum IPC 1 when no multi-cycle instruction stalls ID/EX
Separate 32-bit instruction and data OBI interfaces

columns.label: CONFIGURATION SPACE
columns.title: One core name, multiple golden builds
bullets: RV32EMC or RV32IMC register/ISA direction
Separate golden configurations for FPGA and ASIC targets
Fine-grained SystemVerilog parameters control optional features
XIF variants exist in the matrix; initial golden v1 builds are non-XIF

content.takeaway: The part number names the core; the configuration name selects ISA, target technology, and optional interfaces.
content.narration: CVE2 cleanly separates family from core. OpenHW forked Ibex in 2023 and named the code base CVE2. Its current named core, CV32E20, targets constrained 32-bit MCU and embedded subsystem use. Stage one fetches instructions; stage two combines decode, register access, execution, and writeback. The specification defines golden RV32E M C and RV32I M C builds for FPGA and ASIC targets. The part number alone cannot carry those configuration choices.

scenes.title: The CV32E4 siblings share a pipeline, not a feature set

content.sceneTitle: The CV32E4 siblings share a pipeline, not a feature set
content.title: P, X and S lead to different integration choices
content.subtitle: All three are 32-bit, four-stage, in-order embedded cores; their differentiators live in current manuals.

rows.technicalFocus: RI5CY/PULP-derived compute and DSP-oriented MCU core
rows.extensionPath: Optional F or Zfinx plus PULP custom extensions
rows.integrationSignal: Selected parameters, released version, compiler support

rows.technicalFocus: Compute core designed for external instruction acceleration
rows.extensionPath: CORE-V-XIF offloads ALU, load/store and CSR operations
rows.integrationSignal: XIF protocol subset, coprocessor latency and memory path

rows.extensionPath: Security features and the documented Xsecure direction
rows.integrationSignal: Privilege modes, ePMP/PMA and threat assumptions

content.note: The shared “CV32E4” prefix tells you family resemblance. It does not make P, X and S software- or integration-equivalent.
content.narration: The four-stage embedded family shows why suffixes matter. CV32E40P preserves RI5CY and PULP lineage and may include F or Zfinx plus PULP custom instructions. CV32E40X exposes CORE-V-XIF, allowing external modules to implement instructions without changing core RTL. CV32E40S targets security systems, with Machine and User privilege support, enhanced protection, and anti-tampering features. The shared prefix predicts width, class, and pipeline; the suffix points to a different integration contract.

scenes.title: CVA6 separates the repository from verified configurations

content.sceneTitle: CVA6 separates the repository from verified configurations
content.title: “A6” describes the code-base direction, not every configuration
content.subtitle: Current CVA6 documentation supports both 32- and 64-bit configurations and family-level single- or dual-issue work.

columns.label: REPOSITORY GRAMMAR
columns.title: CVA6 and CV64A60
bullets: CV = CORE-V family
A6 = application class plus six-stage pipeline in the repository name
CV64A60 = 64-bit, application, six stages, product ID 0
The RTL is heavily parameterized; the repository “as is” is not one production core

columns.label: CURRENT CONFIGURATION TABLE
columns.title: Names must be read with their rows
bullets: CV32A60AX: 32-bit application configuration, M/S/U and CV-X-IF
CV32A60X: 32-bit embedded configuration, Machine mode and CV-X-IF
CV64A6_MMU: 64-bit configuration with MMU and M/S/U
The user guide retains an interim-name note; newer index/release pages also expose CV32A65X and CV32A60X 6.0.0

content.takeaway: CVA6 can host cores with different width, privilege, ISA and issue decisions; quote the configuration, not only the repository.
content.narration: CVA6 breaks simplistic decoding. Its repository name indicates CORE-V, application direction, and six stages; CV64A60 is the formal naming example. The user guide lists configurations with different width, privilege, ISA, and targets, and still calls CV32A60X interim. Newer evidence matters: Releases now includes CV32A60X 6.0.0, while the documentation index links CV32A65X. Read the name together with source date and release.

actions.text: Use the decoder after learning the families. CVE2 is a family and repository label; CV32E20 adds width and product identity. CV32E40 siblings share a 32-bit embedded four-stage prefix, while P, X, and S route to different manuals. CVA6 names the configurable repository; CV64A60 is its formal part-number example. CV32A60AX comes from the configuration table, while the current index separately links CV32A65X. Resolve the remaining identifier through the matching document and release.

scenes.title: Silicon identity continues where the name stops

content.sceneTitle: Silicon identity continues where the name stops
content.title: Name, release tag and identity CSRs form one chain
content.subtitle: A production claim should resolve from the human label to a frozen RTL release and machine-readable identifiers.

rows.owner: Architecture ID assigned through RISC-V International

rows.example: CV32E40Pv1 0x0; v2 0x1 in the current catalog

rows.purpose: Pins the exact source baseline used for verification/integration.

content.note: For a reproducible integration record all four: core/configuration name, repository, release/tag, and CSR identities.
content.narration: Human names lead into release identity. OpenHW records a JEDEC value in mvendorid, an architecture ID in marchid, and an implementation ID in mimpid. The current catalog lists architecture IDs for E40P, E40X, E40S, and E20, while E40P versions one and two have different implementation IDs. A Git tag or RTL freeze then pins exact source. This chain is stronger than a slide title or repository default branch.

actions.text: The checkpoint now tests practical classification and lookup. First separate the family or code base from a named core. Then decode CV32E20 without turning the part number into a complete specification. Identify CORE-V-XIF as the defining integration path of CV32E40X. Finally select the three identity CSRs that belong in a release-level hardware check.

scenes.title: A compact lookup method for CORE-V names

content.sceneTitle: A compact lookup method for CORE-V names
content.title: Classify, decode, resolve, then pin the release
takeaways: Classify the label first: family/repository, named core, configuration, or release.
Decode only fields supported by that project’s current documentation.
Use the configuration table for ISA, privilege, interfaces, issue width, and target.
Record repository tag plus mvendorid, marchid, and mimpid for reproducibility.
content.nextStep: Compare the CV32E20 configuration table with the CV32E40X CORE-V-XIF chapter.
content.closing: The name gets you to the right evidence; the evidence defines the core.
content.narration: The engineering method is now compact. First classify the label. Second decode only the fields that the current project or clearly marked historical grammar supports. Third resolve the name to a configuration table and user manual before claiming ISA, privilege, interface, issue width, or maturity. Fourth pin the repository release and the three identity CSRs. With that method, CVE2, CV32E20, the CV32E40 siblings, and CVA6 become a navigable product system rather than a list of cryptic names.
